faq.a: They use simpler reagents and smaller sample volumes, so variability and interference are higher.
faq.q: Why are point‑of‑care tests less precise than central lab assays?

faq.a: Improper sample collection leading to hemolysis or clotting.
faq.q: What is the most common pre‑analytical error?

faq.a: Use urine output monitoring and the bedside creatinine dipstick; track trends rather than single values.
faq.q: How can I estimate kidney function without a creatinine machine?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with fever, jaundice and dark urine presents; which bedside test would you order first and why? — Rapid malaria antigen test; malaria is common and can cause hemolysis leading to jaundice.

You receive a serum creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL in a patient with oliguria; what does this tell you and what is your next step? — Indicates acute kidney injury; give isotonic fluids, stop nephrotoxins and arrange repeat creatinine in 12 h.

A newborn has a total bilirubin of 16 mg/dL; what management is indicated and what threshold would change your plan? — Start phototherapy; if bilirubin rises above 20 mg/dL, consider exchange transfusion.

A patient’s glucose meter reads 65 mg/dL but they are asymptomatic; what could explain the result and what would you do? — Possible interference from anemia or hematocrit; repeat with a laboratory method or check sample quality.
How does hemolysis affect AST and LDH results and how can you recognise it? — Both rise spuriously; look for pink/red plasma and repeat the test with a fresh sample.
Why must a positive rapid HIV test be confirmed, and what is the confirmatory test? — Rapid tests have false‑positive rates; confirm with ELISA or Western blot.
In a malaria‑endemic area, a febrile child has a negative rapid test; what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform thick and thin blood smear microscopy to rule out low‑parasite‑density infection.
What quality‑control measures can you perform on a handheld haemoglobin analyser? — Run control strips each shift, compare with known standards, document any drift.
ai.title: Laboratory Principles in Clinical Biochemistry
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Understanding how common bedside laboratory tests are generated, interpreted and limited helps clinicians diagnose, monitor and triage patients in low‑resource settings.

b: Tests measure substrates, products or enzymes in blood, urine or other fluids.
Results are expressed as concentrations, ratios or activity units.
sections.p: Laboratory principles describe the chemical and enzymatic reactions that underlie the tests we order. In low‑resource hospitals, the same concepts apply whether the assay is run on a point‑of‑care device or a central lab.

b: Spectrophotometry: absorbance change proportional to concentration (e.g., bilirubin).
Electrochemistry: current change for glucose, electrolytes.
Immunoassay: antibody‑antigen binding gives a measurable signal (e.g., HIV rapid test).
sections.p: Most bedside tests use colour change, electrochemical detection or immuno‑capture to quantify an analyte. Accuracy depends on sample quality, reagent stability and calibration.

b: Run internal controls each shift.
Document reagent lot numbers and temperature storage.
sections.p: Quality control (QC) and external quality assessment (EQA) ensure reliability. In low‑resource settings, simple QC (duplicate runs, control strips) is essential.

b: Hemolysis releases intracellular enzymes → spuriously high AST/LDH.
High triglycerides cause turbidity → falsely low glucose on some meters.
sections.p: Pre‑analytical errors (poor collection, hemolysis) are the commonest cause of inaccurate results. Analytical interferences (e.g., bilirubin, lipemia) can falsely raise or lower values.

b: Elevated creatinine with oliguria → acute kidney injury; consider dehydration, sepsis, nephrotoxins.
Low hemoglobin with malaria endemicity → consider hemolysis, iron deficiency, sickle cell disease.
sections.p: Interpretation must link the result to the patient’s presentation, local disease prevalence and test limitations. Recognising patterns guides diagnosis and urgency.

t.b: Is the patient hypoglycaemic? – Result <70 mg/dL confirms hypoglycaemia; if unavailable, use urine dipstick for glucose or bedside capillary sample.
Is there renal dysfunction? – Result ≥1.5 mg/dL suggests AKI; if no chemistry analyser, use bedside creatinine test strips or estimate GFR from urine output.
Is malaria causing fever? – Positive result confirms infection; if unavailable, rely on thick smear microscopy or clinical algorithm.
Is there jaundice from hemolysis or liver disease? – Result ≥2.5 mg/dL indicates clinically significant jaundice; if no spectrophotometer, use visual assessment and urine colour.

t.a: Full blood count (CBC) on handheld analyser
t.b: Is anaemia present? – Hemoglobin <11 g/dL in adults signals anaemia; if device unavailable, use haemoglobin colour scale.

b: Acute kidney injury: give isotonic fluids, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, monitor creatinine trend.
Severe malaria: start artesunate promptly; repeat rapid test to confirm clearance.
Hyperbilirubinaemia in newborns: start phototherapy if total bilirubin ≥15 mg/dL (term) or ≥10 mg/dL (preterm).
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; use laboratory data to guide supportive measures and monitor response.

b: Hemolysis vs true elevated AST – check sample colour and repeat test.
Lipemia vs hypertriglyceridaemia – turbidity may mask glucose; use a cleared sample.
sections.p: Distinguish laboratory artefacts from true pathology.

b: Bilirubin assay interfered by high lipids – may read low; consider dilution.
Glucose meter error in severe anaemia – may underestimate; confirm with laboratory method.
sections.p: Be aware of conditions that alter test accuracy.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in creatinine >0.5 mg/dL within 24 h
Severe hypoglycaemia <40 mg/dL with altered mental status
